papers.title: Spatial GNN Analyzer: An AI-Powered Graph Neural Network Framework for Spatial Transcriptomics Domain Analysis and Visualization
papers.summary: This paper introduces Spatial GNN Analyzer, a software framework that uses graph neural networks to identify and visualize distinct spatial domains within spatial transcriptomics data. It aims to make complex spatial gene expression patterns easier to detect and interpret by leveraging AI-driven graph-based modeling. The tool is positioned as a practical resource for researchers analyzing tissue architecture from spatial omics datasets.
papers.why: Since this PhD work involves spatial transcriptomics analysis using AI/deep learning tools, a GNN-based framework for domain detection could directly support mapping interneuron and perineuronal net-related spatial gene expression patterns in brain tissue.
papers.figure: A figure showing example spatial domain segmentation output overlaid on tissue sections, illustrating how the GNN framework partitions spatial transcriptomic data into distinct domains.

papers.title: Spreading of α-synuclein rewires organelle communication and disrupts neuron-astrocyte mitochondrial quality control
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the spreading of α-synuclein, a protein linked to Parkinson's disease, disrupts communication between organelles within brain cells. It shows that α-synuclein pathology interferes with mitochondrial quality control processes that normally involve cooperation between neurons and astrocytes. The findings suggest that damaged mitochondria are not properly cleared or exchanged between these cell types when α-synuclein spreads, potentially contributing to neurodegeneration.
papers.why: This work directly relates to mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in neurons, extending the picture to neuron-astrocyte interactions that could inform how organelle communication defects intersect with autophagy pathways relevant to the PhD project.

papers.title: Mechanisms underlying perfluorooctanoic acid-induced neuronal loss and cognitive deficits: Disruption of mitochondrial dynamics, impaired mitophagy, and blood-brain barrier dysfunction.
papers.summary: This study investigates how perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), a persistent environmental pollutant, damages the brain by disrupting mitochondrial dynamics and impairing mitophagy, the process cells use to clear damaged mitochondria. It also examines how PFOA compromises the blood-brain barrier, which normally protects the brain from harmful substances. Together, these mechanisms are proposed to explain PFOA-induced neuronal loss and the resulting cognitive deficits observed in exposed subjects.
papers.why: This paper provides direct mechanistic evidence linking impaired mitophagy and mitochondrial dynamics to neuronal loss, offering a toxicological model relevant to understanding mitophagy dysfunction in neurons within the broader context of this PhD research.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1/Parkin or LC3-mitochondria colocalization) alongside neuronal loss and blood-brain barrier integrity measures across PFOA exposure conditions.

papers.title: A combined stimulus of acute fasting and exercise modulates hippocampal mitochondrial quality control in healthy mice.
papers.summary: This study examines how combining short-term fasting with exercise affects mitochondrial quality control in the hippocampus of healthy mice. Mitochondrial quality control includes processes like mitophagy, biogenesis, and dynamics that keep mitochondria functioning properly in neurons. The researchers likely measured markers of these pathways to see if the combined stimulus produces synergistic effects on brain mitochondrial health compared to either intervention alone.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it directly investigates mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in hippocampal neurons, offering physiological triggers and molecular markers that could inform mechanistic studies on neuronal mitophagy relevant to the PhD project.
papers.figure: A figure showing quantification of mitophagy/autophagy markers (e.g., LC3-II, PINK1, Parkin, or BNIP3) across fasting, exercise, and combined treatment groups in hippocampal tissue.

papers.title: Mitochondria-targeted reactive species scavenger JP4-039 protects against disturbances of redox homeostasis, mitochondrial quality control, and glucose metabolism in brains of glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase-deficient mice: A potential new therapeutic strategy for glutaric acidemia type 1.
papers.summary: This study looks at glutaric acidemia type 1, a genetic disease caused by a missing enzyme (glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase) that leads to toxic buildup and brain damage. The researchers tested a drug called JP4-039, which targets mitochondria and mops up harmful reactive molecules, in mice lacking this enzyme. They found the drug helped restore normal redox balance, improved mitochondrial quality control, and normalized glucose metabolism in the brain, suggesting it could be a promising new treatment approach.
papers.why: Although focused on a metabolic disease rather than neurons/interneurons directly, this paper is relevant because it demonstrates how a mitochondria-targeted therapy influences mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control in the brain, which connects directly to the mechanistic focus of the PhD project.
papers.figure: A figure showing brain mitochondrial quality control markers (e.g., mitophagy proteins) and glucose metabolism measures before and after JP4-039 treatment.

papers.title: Integrating UHPLC-HRMS with SSA-BP neural network identifies optimal components of Astragali Radix‑Salviae Miltiorrhizae combination for mitigating cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury via mitophagy and ferroptosis pathways.
papers.summary: This study combines high-resolution mass spectrometry chemical profiling with a machine learning model (SSA-optimized backpropagation neural network) to pinpoint which components of a traditional herbal combination (Astragali Radix and Salviae Miltiorrhizae) are most effective against brain damage caused by stroke-like ischemia-reperfusion injury. The authors link these active compounds to two cell death/survival pathways: mitophagy (clearance of damaged mitochondria) and ferroptosis (iron-dependent cell death). The AI model helps predict and rank which chemical components are likely driving the protective effects, potentially guiding future drug optimization.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it directly connects mitophagy pathways to neuronal injury and uses an AI/deep-learning approach to identify bioactive compounds, offering methodological and mechanistic parallels for analyzing mitophagy-related data in brain tissue.
papers.figure: A figure showing the SSA-BP neural network's predicted correlation between specific chemical components and mitophagy/ferroptosis marker expression in ischemic brain tissue.

papers.title: Impaired mitochondrial quality control and stress signalling machinery modulate senescence induction by genotoxic challenge.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how defects in mitochondrial quality control and stress signalling pathways influence whether cells undergo senescence in response to DNA-damaging (genotoxic) stress. It likely explores the crosstalk between mitochondrial health, autophagic/mitophagic clearance mechanisms, and cellular stress responses like the DNA damage response. The findings probably show that when mitochondrial quality control is impaired, cells are more prone to entering a senescent state after genotoxic insult.
papers.why: Since senescence and mitochondrial quality control are tightly linked to mitophagy dysfunction, this work could inform how impaired mitochondrial clearance in neurons contributes to age- or stress-related decline relevant to interneuron vulnerability.

papers.title: Integrative phosphoproteomics reveals kinase-mediated regulation of OCIAD1 and its roles in mitochondrial quality control.
papers.summary: This study uses phosphoproteomics to map how kinases add phosphate groups to the protein OCIAD1, a mitochondria-associated protein. The researchers show that this phosphorylation controls OCIAD1's function in mitochondrial quality control, a process that helps cells identify and remove damaged mitochondria. Their findings link specific kinase signaling pathways to mitochondrial health maintenance mechanisms.
papers.why: Since mitophagy is central to this PhD project, understanding kinase-mediated regulation of mitochondrial quality control proteins like OCIAD1 could reveal new molecular targets or pathways relevant to neuronal mitophagy regulation.
